sections.heading: 1. A title outside the official record
sections.text:
On 5 September 1971, Denmark defeated Mexico 3–0 at the Estadio Azteca in Mexico City. Susanne Augustesen, a 15-year-old schoolgirl from Holbæk, scored every Danish goal. Denmark’s football association, DBU, describes a crowd of 110,000. This was a major sporting occasion, played in the stadium that had hosted the men’s World Cup final a year earlier.

Yet the competition was not organised by FIFA. Calling Denmark champions of the 1971 unofficial women’s world tournament is accurate; calling them winners of a FIFA Women’s World Cup is not. Both the achievement and the distinction matter. The players competed internationally before the institutions that governed much of football had built equivalent opportunities for women. Their story asks us to examine what an official record includes, and what it leaves outside.

sections.heading: 2. From a club invitation to a national selection
sections.text:
The journey had roots in club football. Boldklubben Femina was founded in 1959, following an initiative by journalist Alf Mørkeberg. In 1970, a strengthened Femina side represented Denmark at an unofficial tournament in Italy and won the final against the hosts 2–0. That earlier success explains why an invitation for the next tournament reached the club.

For Mexico, however, the approach changed. The Danish women’s football union, DKFU, took responsibility for the invitation, and a selection committee chose a squad of 16 from clubs around Denmark. Only Helene Østergaard Hansen had also been part of the victorious 1970 team. Denmark therefore defended its title with a substantially different squad. The continuity lay in the achievement represented by the name Denmark, rather than an unchanged group of players.

sections.heading: 3. Two cities and more than one goalscorer
sections.text:
Six teams entered the Mexico tournament. Denmark played its group matches at the Estadio Jalisco in Guadalajara, opening with a 3–0 win over France and then drawing 1–1 with Italy. The knockout matches took the Danes to the Estadio Azteca in Mexico City, where they beat Argentina 5–0 in the semi-final.

Augustesen’s final hat-trick can dominate a short account, but it does not explain every earlier result. Lis Lene Nielsen scored twice against France and three times against Argentina. Those five goals made her the tournament’s leading scorer, according to the Danish reference work Lex. Augustesen had scored the other goal against France. A reader who remembers only the most famous performance could easily confuse the final’s outstanding scorer with the leading scorer across the competition.

sections.heading: 4. A teenager decides the final
sections.text:
The final brought Denmark up against the host nation. Augustesen scored in the 26th minute, then added goals in the 52nd and 62nd minutes. Denmark won 3–0. Her three goals arrived across both halves: the first established a lead, while the next two extended it after the interval. The score records a decisive result without requiring us to invent a speech, private thought or tactical instruction.

The scale of the setting also matters. A Danish schoolgirl had performed before an enormous crowd at one of football’s best-known grounds. Her age makes the achievement striking, but she was part of a selected team whose route included contributions from several scorers. Remembering both the individual and the collective gives a fuller explanation of how Denmark reached that day.

sections.heading: 5. Celebration and recognition were different events
sections.text:
The team returned to public celebration, including a reception with pancakes at Copenhagen’s city hall. Nevertheless, a successful tournament did not instantly produce the same institutional status that men’s football enjoyed. In February 1972, DBU admitted women’s football. Denmark’s first official women’s international followed in 1974.

These dates describe separate milestones. Winning in Mexico, entering DBU and playing an official international were not three names for the same event. Nor did the later milestones mean that football played beforehand had never happened. The distinction helps explain how pioneers can be celebrated for performances that do not appear in the same statistical series as later official matches. Historical recognition involves more than preserving a result: it also involves explaining the system used to classify it.

sections.heading: 6. Augustesen’s career continued elsewhere
sections.text:
Italian clubs wanted Augustesen after Mexico, but she and her parents agreed that she would wait until she was 18 before moving abroad. In 1974, she chose a football opportunity in Italy rather than pursuing her promising handball pathway. Her later career included six Italian championships, eight seasons as Serie A’s leading scorer and more than 600 goals overall, as reported by UEFA.

Despite those achievements, DBU records no official senior Denmark appearances for her. That makes her career a useful test of how we judge evidence. An official international appearance total describes selection within a particular system. On its own, it cannot tell us everything about a player’s ability, club success or earlier unofficial international performances. Augustesen’s record requires those different strands to be read together.

sections.heading: 7. What remembering the team changes
sections.text:
Augustesen entered Denmark’s football Hall of Fame in 2017, alongside Lone Smidt Nielsen, when the first women players were inducted. The 1971 squad received its own Hall of Fame recognition in 2019. These honours came decades after the final. They made space within Danish football’s public memory for achievements that younger supporters might otherwise miss.

The first FIFA Women’s World Cup was held in China in 1991, twenty years after Denmark’s Mexico victory. Neither event needs to erase the other. One marks the beginning of FIFA’s championship; the other demonstrates an earlier international competition that women had already made possible. Reading this history carefully means keeping the chronology straight, recognising different forms of achievement, and asking which evidence supports each claim.

name: Arsenal 2007
subtitle: The quadruple

artwork.front: STAR Ultimate Challenge UC02. Arsenal 2007, The Quadruple. Modern scarlet red, midnight navy and chrome card with a sharp photorealistic reconstructed celebration. artwork.back: Arsenal 2007 Ultimate Challenge UC02. Matching modern scarlet, navy and chrome design. Perfect league record: 22 wins from 22, 119 goals scored, ten conceded and 66 points. sections.heading: 1. Four competitions, one campaign
sections.text:
In 2006–07, Arsenal Ladies won the FA Women’s Premier League National Division, the FA Women’s Premier League Cup, the FA Women’s Cup and the UEFA Women’s Cup. These four major titles form the quadruple. The European competition was the predecessor of today’s Women’s Champions League, rather than a separate fifth trophy to add to the list.

Manager Vic Akers had founded the women’s team in 1987. Its greatest campaign therefore arrived twenty years into a much longer project. That background matters: a historic season can look like a sudden burst of success when it is remembered through trophy photographs. Arsenal’s achievement also rested on an established team and years of development. To understand the quadruple, we need to follow several competitions, rather than imagine that one match decided everything.

sections.heading: 2. Perfect means more than unbeaten
sections.text:
Arsenal finished their league programme with 22 victories from 22 matches. They scored 119 goals, conceded ten and collected 66 points. Everton, the runners-up, finished on 52 points. The final table therefore shows both attacking production and a fourteen-point gap at the top.

A perfect winning record is a more precise description than simply unbeaten. An unbeaten team can draw matches; Arsenal did not. Their goal difference was plus 109, calculated by subtracting ten conceded from 119 scored. These numbers describe the league campaign, not every match played that season. That distinction will matter when we reach Europe: the second leg of the continental final ended in a draw. Winning every league game did not mean winning every individual fixture in every competition.

sections.heading: 3. Leeds make the League Cup difficult
sections.text:
On 4 March 2007, Arsenal faced Leeds United at Glanford Park in Scunthorpe. Jayne Ludlow captained Arsenal while Faye White was injured. Leeds resisted strongly, and the match remained goalless as extra time approached. Arsenal’s reputation and league scoring rate had not settled this final.

Ludlow eventually volleyed in Karen Carney’s corner in the second minute of stoppage time. Arsenal won 1–0. The decisive combination involved a delivery from Carney and a finish from Ludlow, with timing as important as the final score. It offers a useful counterweight to the league statistics. A team capable of scoring freely across a season still needed persistence, a set-piece opportunity and a very late breakthrough to win this particular trophy.

sections.heading: 4. An advantage earned in Sweden
sections.text:
The UEFA Women’s Cup final was played over two legs against Sweden’s Umeå IK. On 21 April, Arsenal travelled to Sweden for the opening match. Their opponents created pressure, especially with a strong wind helping them in the first half. Arsenal held out before right-back Alex Scott scored in added time to secure a 1–0 away win.

This was also a test of adaptability. Defensive absences had required players such as midfielder Anita Asante to change positions. The first-leg result was therefore more than an attacking highlight. It combined defensive work with Scott’s late strike. A one-goal advantage made Arsenal favourites to complete the task, but it did not finish the final. Another full match still separated them from the European trophy.

sections.heading: 5. A goalless match that won a trophy
sections.text:
The return leg took place at Meadow Park in Borehamwood on 29 April. Arsenal drew 0–0, making the aggregate score 1–0 in their favour. Goalkeeper Emma Byrne produced important saves. Umeå also hit the post through Ramona Bachmann and the crossbar through Marta late in the match. Arsenal had chances themselves, but no further goal was added.

Jayne Ludlow led the side before Faye White came on in the final minute; both helped lift the trophy. Kelly Smith had missed the European triumph through suspension. This was a collective achievement involving players in different circumstances. The aggregate score explains why a draw could secure a title. Scott scored the tie’s only goal in Sweden; Byrne and her team-mates then helped protect that advantage at home.

sections.heading: 6. Coming from behind to complete the four
sections.text:
Eight days later, on 7 May, Arsenal met Charlton Athletic in the FA Cup final at Nottingham’s City Ground. Katie Holtham put Charlton ahead after two minutes. Kelly Smith equalised five minutes later from a free-kick. Ludlow then scored twice before half-time, and Smith added Arsenal’s fourth in the second half. Arsenal won 4–1, with two goals each from Smith and Ludlow.

That victory completed the four major titles. Notice the change in Smith’s role: unavailable for the European triumph, she was a scorer in the match that secured the quadruple. Lianne Sanderson supplied the free-kick for Ludlow’s first goal, while Katie Chapman provided the pass for Smith’s second. The scoreline belongs alongside those contributions, rather than replacing them.

sections.heading: 7. Reading the achievement accurately
sections.text:
Arsenal still had two league fixtures remaining after the FA Cup final, although the league title was already secure. Wins against Everton and Leeds subsequently completed the perfect league record. The quadruple was therefore secured before the final league statistics were complete. Keeping those two moments separate prevents an easy chronological mistake.

Across the campaign, different tasks demanded different responses: sustained league consistency, a stoppage-time League Cup winner, protection of an aggregate European lead and recovery from an early FA Cup setback. These are lessons we can draw from the results, rather than claims about private team conversations. When judging a historic team, ask what each record actually measures. Four major trophies describe the season’s honours; 22 wins describe its league programme; one away goal explains the European final.

sections.heading: 1. A professional dream
sections.text:
In 2000, Fulham’s women became full-time professionals. That decision changed the conditions in which the players could pursue their football: the club was building an ambitious team around paid, full-time work in a game where that opportunity was unusual. English internationals such as Rachel Yankey and Katie Chapman played alongside overseas talent, including Norway’s Marianne Pettersen. The project was about reaching the top, rather than simply attaching a famous men’s club name to a women’s team.

Their rise still involved promotion. Fulham won the South East Combination and reached the 2001 FA Cup final. This matters when reading their later achievements: they did not begin the professional experiment as champions of the highest division. The team had to climb towards that position, turning resources and individual ability into results.

sections.heading: 2. Numbers that need their context
sections.text:
The next step was the Premier League Southern Division in 2001–02. Fulham won all 22 league matches, scoring 234 goals and conceding only six. Their biggest league victory was 22–0 against Barking. Pettersen scored 79 goals across all competitions. Manager Gaute Haugenes had a squad containing experienced internationals, and the results exposed a huge competitive gap between this full-time team and many opponents.

They also won the FA Cup and League Cup that season. However, the league title in that collection was the Southern Division title, not the top-flight National Division championship. Keeping those competitions separate prevents a misleading retelling of the story. The extraordinary scoring record demonstrated dominance at that stage of the climb; it did not mean Fulham had already won England’s highest league.

sections.heading: 3. The challenge at the top
sections.text:
In 2002–03, Fulham entered the National Division. They began by beating Doncaster Belles 4–0, but the season was not simply a repeat of their perfect Southern Division campaign. Charlton Athletic held them to draws, and Arsenal provided a serious rival. A 2–1 win at Arsenal, with both Fulham goals scored by Kristy Moore, helped establish the newcomers as genuine title contenders.

This was a different kind of test from overwhelming teams by enormous margins. Against strong opposition, a decisive contribution could come in a tight match rather than a procession of goals. For a reader following the journey, the important change is the level of competition: Fulham now had to prove that their earlier success could survive the move into the highest division.

sections.heading: 4. A final that refused to finish
sections.text:
The League Cup final against Arsenal on 30 March 2003 tested their response to a sudden setback. Rachel Yankey scored in the 89th minute, putting Fulham within touching distance of the trophy. Ciara Grant equalised with seconds remaining. Extra time produced no further goals, so a match Fulham had nearly won in normal time went to penalties.

Goalkeeper Astrid Johannessen made four shoot-out saves, and Kim Jerray-Silver converted the decisive penalty. Fulham won the shoot-out 3–2 after the 1–1 draw. Those are two different scores describing two different parts of the contest. The result also gives a more demanding picture of their success: they needed to recover emotionally, continue through extra time and perform under pressure after a late equaliser had taken away an apparent victory.

sections.heading: 5. Completing the treble

sections.heading: 1. A club ready for a bigger stage
sections.text:
When England’s first national women’s league began in 1991, Doncaster Belles were already a formidable club. Founded in 1969, they had built their reputation through regional football and repeated appearances in the national cup final. Sheila Edmunds, born Sheila Stocks, was a key founder and long-serving player. The move to a national competition offered something the Belles had wanted: strong opponents on a more regular basis.

That distinction matters. Their story did not begin when a new league gave them a national platform. Years of work had prepared them for it. Sheila later explained that switching between comfortable regional fixtures and much tougher cup ties created its own difficulties. A national league could provide a more consistent challenge. The Belles arrived with ambition, experience and a team ready to measure itself against the best.

sections.heading: 2. Fourteen matches, fourteen wins
sections.text:
The 1991–92 WFA National League Premier Division season produced an extraordinary record. Doncaster won all 14 league games, scored 89 goals and conceded only four. They opened with a 4–0 victory over Millwall Lionesses and followed it with a 7–0 away win at Ipswich Town. By the end, they were the first champions of this new national competition.

Brian Broadhurst managed the team that season while Paul Edmunds took a year away from the role to study. The change did not prevent a perfect league campaign. It is important to understand what perfect means here: fourteen victories, rather than simply avoiding defeat. An unbeaten side can draw matches. These Belles did not drop a league point. Their achievement combined attacking force with a defence that allowed very few goals.

sections.heading: 3. A scorer and the team around her

Karen Walker was central to that success. The striker scored 36 league goals in the fourteen-match campaign. She also produced an exceptional cup run, scoring a hat-trick in every round, including the final. Doncaster beat Red Star Southampton 4–0 at Prenton Park to complete the 1991–92 league-and-cup double.

The National Football Museum’s account of Walker’s career records both the scoring feat and the double. Yet an individual total should not make the rest of the team disappear from the story. sections.heading: 4. Rivals change the challenge
sections.text:
Winning the first national title did not give Doncaster permanent ownership of the competition. Arsenal won the following season’s league and beat the Belles in the 1993 cup final. The final score was 3–0. For Doncaster, returning to the top would therefore involve responding to a rival that had already taken both prizes from them.

The 1993–94 campaign was also part of a wider change in the women’s game: the Football Association completed its takeover of the national league. In the cup, the 1994 competition was the first under the FA’s direct control of women’s football. Doncaster’s two doubles belong to this period of transition. Competition names and administrators changed, but the players still had to earn results on the field. The story links an established club with the developing structure of the national game.

sections.heading: 5. A narrow final and a difficult finish
sections.text:
Doncaster reclaimed the cup with a 1–0 victory over Knowsley United at Glanford Park in 1994. Karen Walker scored the only goal. It was a very different winning margin from the 4–0 final two years earlier, but the trophy was the same national cup. A team’s quality cannot always be read from the size of its winning margin.

The league was still to be secured. A 3–1 defeat at Arsenal left the Belles needing nine points from their remaining four matches. They responded by winning all four in just twelve days, with an aggregate score of 24–2. The sequence turned a damaging defeat into a championship-winning finish. Their 1993–94 league campaign produced 110 goals in eighteen matches and another double. This time, the route to success included a setback close to the end.

sections.heading: 6. The double was not a treble
sections.text:
There is an easy trap when remembering a great team: assuming that every trophy went their way. Doncaster’s 1993–94 double consisted of the league and FA Cup. The League Cup was a separate competition, and its final was delayed until 13 November 1994 because the previous season had run out of time to stage it.

When that final was played at Cambridge United’s Abbey Stadium, Arsenal won 4–0 against an injury-hit Belles side. The calendar date and the competition’s season label do not match neatly, so careful reading matters. A final played in November 1994 could still belong to the 1993–94 competition. Including the defeat makes the history more accurate. It does not remove the league and cup that Doncaster had already earned, or reduce the achievement of recovering to win them.

sections.heading: 7. What the golden years teach us
sections.text:
The two doubles reveal different forms of excellence. In 1991–92, Doncaster won every league match. In 1993–94, they recovered from a late defeat and completed a demanding run of fixtures. Both routes ended with the league and cup, but the experiences along the way were different.

For STAR players, our interpretation is that a setback deserves a response, not an instant verdict on a player or team. Doncaster’s return offers an example to think about, rather than a promise that determination always brings a trophy. Good players can lose finals. Great teams can need help, time and another attempt. Remembering the Belles accurately means keeping the defeats alongside the achievements, recognising the people behind the results, and understanding why their place in women’s football was built over years.

sections.heading: 1. A team before the invasion
sections.text:
Mariupol Women’s FC existed long before its players had to explain what it meant to lose their home. Karina Kulakovska and Yana Vynokurova co-founded the club in 2015. They were building a football team with ambitions, routines and a place in the Ukrainian game. Keeping that earlier history in view matters: the women were athletes before they became subjects of wartime reporting.

The club also worked to make its matches visible. A 2022 account of its equipment appeal records that Mariupol had joined Singular Live’s support scheme for non-profit organisations in 2021. Matches had been streamed on YouTube. These details show a club trying to develop its audience and resources, not a team invented later as a symbol. War interrupted a project that people had already spent years creating.

sections.heading: 2. From football plans to a basement
sections.text:
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. In Mariupol, members of the team took shelter in the basement of Vynokurova’s house. Her testimony, recorded by the Museum of Civilian Voices, describes a shell striking the yard and the decision to leave. A small car carried seven people, five cats and a dog out of the city.

Those details come from a participant’s account, rather than an imagined scene written for this card. They describe a frightening civilian escape, not an adventurous team trip. The distinction is important when reading sporting stories about war. Losing access to a pitch was only one part of what happened. The immediate concern was staying alive and reaching somewhere safer, with teammates and the animals in their care.

sections.heading: 3. Helping other people leave
sections.text:
Leaving Mariupol did not end the involvement of the club’s leaders with people still trapped there. Vynokurova and Kulakovska returned with humanitarian supplies and helped evacuate civilians. The Museum of Civilian Voices records that return; Vynokurova also described the journey and the help of a bus driver in an interview with Arab News in April 2023.

The interview explains how neighbours and other civilians became part of the reason to go back. It also describes the psychological cost afterwards, including Vynokurova seeking professional support. That is part of the history too. Courage does not mean that someone feels no fear or needs no help. Their actions should not become a demand that other survivors take similar risks. The account belongs to these people and the choices they faced.

sections.heading: 4. Rebuilding needed ordinary equipment
sections.text:
By August 2022, an appeal supported by Singular Live set out what restarting football required. Mariupol needed boots, shirts, nets and cones. The request also covered equipment and people to help broadcast matches. Players had scattered across Europe, and the club intended to return to Ukraine for the new season.

The list makes the scale of rebuilding concrete. A remembered name or a determination to continue cannot supply boots, mark out a training exercise or operate a camera. Practical support turns an intention into something people can do. The media appeal had a purpose alongside the playing equipment: the club wanted its games to be seen. However, an appeal announcing a planned return is evidence of intention at that moment. It is not, by itself, proof that competitive matches have already resumed.

sections.heading: 5. Keeping Mariupol on the team sheet
sections.text:
Some of the club’s core members initially found refuge in Bulgaria. They later returned to Ukraine and rebuilt from a base in Kyiv. Other clubs and individuals donated equipment. The squad included players from different parts of the country, alongside a small group from the original Mariupol team. Its city’s name continued with them.

In April 2023, AP reporting described the club’s wish to remain visible and retain its connection to Mariupol. Continuing was about more than chasing a championship. A club can carry memories, relationships and a public identity when its members cannot play at home. That does not mean every new recruit had the same experiences as the original players. A rebuilt squad contains different histories, even when everyone wears the same badge.

sections.heading: 6. A return shown in the results
sections.text:
Official competition records provide a different kind of evidence from a rebuilding appeal. The Ukrainian Association of Football’s report for the fifteenth round of the 2022–23 women’s Premier League lists Atex Kyiv against Mariupol on 1 April 2023. The match finished 0–0. Mariupol’s name was back in an ordinary league result, alongside the other fixtures.

That draw did not settle the club’s future, but it did show participation in competitive football. Returning to play also did not remove wartime danger. In November 2023, an air-raid warning interrupted a Mariupol match; players took shelter. It is possible for football to resume while life remains deeply disrupted. Playing again and being safely back to normal are different claims, and the evidence supports treating them separately.

sections.heading: 7. More than an easy resilience story
sections.text:
Mariupol’s 2022–23 story has no simple ending in which a trophy repairs everything that was lost. Its significance lies in people surviving, helping others and rebuilding enough of their club to compete again. The available accounts describe a particular period; they do not establish that the team’s later problems had all been solved.

By August 2022, an appeal supported by Singular Live set out what restarting football required. Mariupol needed boots, shirts, nets and cones. name: Sudan: Samidat
subtitle: The game they carried

artwork.front: STAR Ultimate Challenge UC06: Sudan, Samidat, The Game They Carried. An illustrated reconstruction of adult Sudanese women footballers in the navy and orange kit documented in April 2025, with a copper frame, Nile and Cairo evening background.
artwork.back: Samidat UC06: Sudan’s 2019 women’s league, the 2023 conflict, the January 2025 Cairo restart and the funding pause reported in July 2025.

sections.heading: 1. A football history before exile
sections.text:
Sudanese women were building football lives long before Samidat existed. Interviews conducted in 2022 by researchers Sara Al-Hassan and Deen Sharp describe players facing restrictions, harassment and social disapproval, while also showing that experiences differed between regions and families. There was no single story shared by every woman.

The first official national women’s league began in 2019. CAF records Al-Difaa beating Al-Tahadi 1–0 in the final that December, watched by nearly six thousand people. Ilham Beltone scored the winner and finished as the competition’s leading scorer. These were organised teams with skilled players, coaches and supporters. Remembering those details gives the later exile story its proper starting point: war disrupted an existing sporting community.

sections.heading: 2. When the pitch became unreachable
sections.text:
UNHCR dates the outbreak of the conflict to 15 April 2023. Fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces drove civilians from their homes, both within Sudan and across its borders. Egypt became a destination for people seeking safety. The footballers who later gathered in Cairo were part of this much wider displacement.

A team can lose more than a ground when its members are forced to leave. Familiar travel routes, training partners and the ordinary expectation of next week’s session can disappear together. That is our interpretation of what displacement means for sporting participation, rather than a claim that every refugee has the same experience. Reaching another country does not automatically provide the time, money or stability needed to play.

sections.heading: 3. A coach with her own pioneering journey
sections.text:
Samidat’s coach, Salma al-Majidi, already had a remarkable football career. AFP reporting in 2018 described her coaching men at Al-Ahly Al-Gadaref, after working with other Sudanese clubs. Her players called her their sister coach. The report also described the resistance she had faced as a woman working in a role often assumed to belong to men.

Her knowledge did not begin with the Cairo project. She brought experience of organising practices, developing players and earning a squad’s trust. That matters when considering who refugee athletes and coaches are: leaving home does not erase their expertise. A rebuilding project can create the conditions for that knowledge to be used again, instead of treating the people involved only as recipients of help.

sections.heading: 4. Thirty women gather again
sections.text:
In January 2025, around thirty Sudanese women footballers regrouped in Cairo as Samidat, a name translated as resilient women. Reporting by Bianca Carrera for More to Her Story identifies Fikra and the Strategic Initiative for Women in the Horn of Africa, known as SIHA, as organisations behind the project. Al-Majidi became its coach.

Several players had competed for Sudanese clubs such as Al-Tahadi and Al-Difaa. They brought memories of competitive football into their new sessions. Carrera’s photographs from 17 April 2025 show a real training group, wearing navy shirts with orange trim and the team’s name across their backs. This card’s artwork is an illustrated reconstruction based on that documented kit, rather than a photograph of a particular player.

sections.heading: 5. Training was a beginning
sections.text:
The May 2025 report described Samidat as unregistered in Egypt’s national league. Their ambition was to arrange friendly matches with Egyptian women’s teams, including a hoped-for meeting with Al-Ahly. A wish to play a fixture is different from a recorded match result. The evidence at that point supports a return to training, rather than entry into official league competition.

That distinction does not make the sessions unimportant. A pass, a shared drill and a coach’s instruction can restore part of an athlete’s routine. It does mean that we should describe progress accurately. Samidat was a Sudanese women’s team rebuilding in exile; this account does not establish that it was an officially recognised replacement for Sudan’s national side.

sections.heading: 6. Determination still needed support
sections.text:
Carrera’s July 2025 follow-up for El Salto described the contribution of Shlail, a sports and arts association, alongside Fikra and SIHA. It also reported a pause in Samidat’s activities because of insufficient funding. The women’s commitment had not made the practical problem disappear. Organisers hoped that further support would allow sessions to resume.

This is a crucial part of the story. Calling athletes resilient should never become an excuse to overlook what enables participation. A team needs access to space, equipment, coaching and the ability to get people together. Those are ordinary football requirements, even when the circumstances are extraordinary. A funding interruption is evidence of a resource problem; it should not be retold as proof that the players lacked ambition.

sections.heading: 7. Carrying the story forward
sections.text:
Samidat’s story also reached documentary audiences. Goldsmiths, University of London, advertised a March 2026 screening of Samidat alongside another film about refugee women. Its event description presented football as a way for Sudanese women in Egypt to express agency, care and collective action. A screening shows that their story was being shared; it does not establish the team’s current playing schedule or financial position.

For STAR players, our interpretation is that belonging depends on opportunities people can actually reach. Listening to these women means recognising both their football ability and the conditions they need to use it. Their history deserves more than an easy ending about overcoming everything. Samidat carried a sporting community into exile, and its future still required practical support.

name: Portsmouth’s Buswomen
subtitle: The game carried on

artwork.front: STAR UC07: Portsmouth’s Buswomen. The game carried on. Illustrated historical reconstruction in period style, with the official STAR mark.
artwork.back: Portsmouth’s Buswomen: a historical summary with dates, context and the seven-question earning requirement.

sections.heading: 1. A Christmas fixture survives
sections.text:
Christmas Day, 1941. Two teams of women bus workers met at Privett Park, in Gosport, across the harbour from Portsmouth. The University of Wolverhampton’s account of wartime women’s football records Hants & Dorset Motor Services conductresses beating the women drivers of Provincial Omnibus 4–3. That compact result preserves a football occasion during an extraordinary year.

Seven goals tell us that both sides scored, and subtraction tells us that the winning margin was one. They do not reveal who led at half-time, whether anyone scored a hat-trick or when the winning goal arrived. Those are tempting ingredients for a dramatic retelling, but this story leaves them open. The surviving account is enough to establish the match without inventing its action.

sections.heading: 2. The year behind the match
sections.text:
Earlier that year, Portsmouth had endured its worst air raid, on the night of 10–11 January. Portsmouth Museum explains how telephone staff in the Air Raid Precautions control room recorded incoming reports and requests for help. Their messages describe fires, damaged roads, trapped people and difficulties sending rescue services.

The museum also warns that the record contains gaps. An event might be absent because a report has not survived, or because someone responded without sending one. That is a useful lesson for football history too: an incomplete archive is not a complete picture of everything people did. These January records establish the danger experienced in the area; they do not prove that a raid interrupted the Christmas match eleven months later.

sections.heading: 3. Workers with a sporting identity
sections.text:
A government account of women’s wartime work lists bus driving alongside engineering, mechanics, munitions production and air raid duties. Women also sustained households under rationing. Work on the home front therefore involved many kinds of responsibility, rather than a single uniform experience.

The fixture’s team descriptions identify two different transport jobs. A conductress worked with passengers and fares; a driver operated the vehicle. The distinction matters because changing the teams into two generic factory sides would erase what makes this particular match recognisable. These women belonged to workplaces, but they also appeared as footballers. Our interpretation is that preserving both identities gives a fuller account of their lives than remembering only their contribution to wartime labour.

sections.heading: 4. A ban was still in place
sections.text:
Historic England dates the FA’s exclusion of women from affiliated grounds from 1921 to 1971. Women continued playing at other venues during those decades. The restriction reduced access to facilities and crowds, but it was not a law making every women’s kickabout or match a criminal offence.

The distinction helps explain how a wartime fixture could exist while exclusion continued. It would be wrong to use the Gosport result as proof that the FA had lifted its policy. It would also be wrong to read the policy as proof that no women played. Rules imposed by a powerful organisation and the activities of people outside its preferred arrangements can appear together in the same historical moment.

sections.heading: 5. What seven goals cannot tell us
sections.text:
A close score invites imagination. Perhaps a goalkeeper made a spectacular save, or a defender found a brave pass. Those possibilities belong to football generally; the account used here does not establish them for this game. Nor does it provide a reliable attendance, a full team sheet or verified kit colours.

The artwork is consequently labelled a reconstruction. Its period clothing, bus and winter setting help communicate an era, rather than supplying new documentary evidence. A convincing picture cannot settle an unanswered historical question. If a team photograph or contemporary match report becomes available, it should be checked against the date and opponents before being used to revise the story. Visual confidence and historical certainty are different things.

sections.heading: 6. A match inside a wider history
sections.text:
Workplace and service football offered ways for women to gather during the war. Yet the meaning of one fixture cannot be stretched to represent every player or every town. We should not assume that all the buswomen had the same background, level of experience or reason for taking part.

Playing might offer competition, companionship or a change from work, but those are interpretations here, not quotations from these women. Likewise, the wider association between wartime sport and fundraising does not identify the recipient of money from this particular match. A careful account keeps its focus: two named groups of transport workers played a recorded game. Their place in football history does not depend on adding an unverified charity total or heroic speech.

sections.heading: 7. Remembering the players
sections.text:
The final score gives Hants & Dorset the victory, while the fixture gives both teams a place in the record. It challenges a familiar shortcut in football history: treating years of official exclusion as years without women’s participation. It also invites us to look beyond celebrated stadiums when asking who kept playing.

For STAR players, the challenge is to read with both curiosity and precision. Remember the workplaces, jobs, location and date; then consider which conclusions follow from them. Respecting the unknown details does not diminish the women. It leaves room for future research and protects their real achievement from becoming a story somebody else invented. On Christmas Day 1941, a football match happened, and its result still allows us to remember it.

sections.heading: 1. A difficult decision
sections.text:
Japan’s 2011 Women’s World Cup began with a question that was much bigger than football. After the earthquake and tsunami of 11 March, would travelling to Germany be the right thing to do? People had lost homes and loved ones. Communities faced long recovery work, while the Fukushima nuclear crisis added further uncertainty.

Midfielder Aya Miyama later recalled discussing participation with her teammates. They decided that playing could offer encouragement to people affected by the disaster. That did not make the tournament a solution to the suffering at home. It gave the players a way to contribute through the skill they shared. Their journey carried both sporting ambition and a feeling of responsibility to people watching from Japan.

sections.heading: 2. A disrupted game at home
sections.text:
The disruption reached the domestic game too. TEPCO Mareeze, a women’s club based near Fukushima, suspended playing activity and withdrew from the top division for the season. Footballers needed somewhere else to train and play. Aya Sameshima, who would start the World Cup final at left-back, joined Boston Breakers in the United States.

The Asian Football Confederation’s account also explains that Japan’s women’s league season began a month late. Many players fitted football around jobs or studies. Their preparation therefore took place within a game already facing practical disruption. Knowing this helps us understand the tournament without imagining that every member of the squad experienced the disaster in exactly the same way.

sections.heading: 3. A plan built around the ball
sections.text:
Coach Norio Sasaki’s team had a football identity as well as a reason to care. Miyama described their work on possession: retaining the ball was a means of competing effectively against opponents who could be bigger physically. Passing had to serve the match, helping Japan keep control and create opportunities.

For a young player, this offers a useful tactical distinction. A team can respond to an opponent’s strengths by choosing different problems to set them. Quick support angles, a secure first touch and a well-timed pass can make physical pressure harder to apply. That is a coaching lesson drawn from Japan’s approach, rather than a claim that technique removes every physical disadvantage. Their football still required effort, organisation and defensive work.

sections.heading: 4. A defeat within a winning journey
sections.text:
Japan beat New Zealand 2–1 and Mexico 4–0 in the group stage. Homare Sawa scored a hat-trick against Mexico. Then came a 2–0 defeat by England. The future champions had lost a match before the knockout rounds began; their title was not an unbeaten march through the tournament.

The quarter-final brought hosts Germany, winners of the previous two World Cups. Japan won 1–0 after extra time, with Karina Maruyama scoring in the 108th minute. Sweden followed in the semi-final. Japan won 3–1, with two goals from Nahomi Kawasumi and one from Sawa. These results show how the team moved from a group-stage setback to victories over formidable opposition. Each match demanded a fresh performance rather than a perfect record.

sections.heading: 5. Twice behind in Frankfurt
sections.text:
The final against the United States took place in Frankfurt on 17 July. Before that match, Japan had failed to beat the Americans in their previous 25 meetings. Alex Morgan put the USA ahead in the second half, and Aya Miyama equalised in the 81st minute. Japan had recovered once, but the final was far from finished.

Abby Wambach restored the American lead during extra time. With the match approaching its end, Sawa scored in the 117th minute to make it 2–2. Japan had come from behind twice. Azusa Iwashimizu was then sent off near the end of extra time. The score remained level, so the trophy would be decided by penalties. Recovery had kept Japan in the contest; it had not yet won it.

sections.heading: 6. The work of a goalkeeper and a team
sections.text:
Ayumi Kaihori saved Shannon Boxx’s opening penalty with an outstretched leg. Carli Lloyd put the next American attempt over the crossbar, and Kaihori stopped Tobin Heath’s kick. These were three unsuccessful USA attempts, but only two were saves by the goalkeeper. That difference matters when telling the story accurately.

Japan also had an unsuccessful kick: Hope Solo saved Yuki Nagasato’s attempt. The shoot-out still ended 3–1 to Japan. Saki Kumagai converted the deciding penalty, completing the victory after the two teams had drawn the match itself. The final score was therefore 2–2 after extra time, with Japan winning the separate penalty shoot-out. Combining those numbers into an ordinary match score would misrepresent what happened.

sections.heading: 7. Recognition beyond one night
sections.text:
Japan became the first Asian winners of the Women’s World Cup. Sawa finished with five goals and received both the Golden Boot as leading scorer and the Golden Ball as the tournament’s outstanding player. The team also received the Fair Play Award.

The Japan Football Association records another distinction: the squad became the first group to receive Japan’s People’s Honour Award. In 2023, the 2011 team was selected for the Japan Football Hall of Fame. These honours recognise a collective achievement as well as exceptional individuals. Miyama’s equaliser, Sawa’s goals, Kaihori’s saves and Kumagai’s final kick belong to the same team story, alongside the contributions of players whose names appear less often in its retelling.

sections.heading: 8. What the story asks of a player
sections.text:
Japan’s achievement can inspire without turning grief into a football lesson. Winning a trophy did not undo the disaster or complete the country’s recovery. It offered a moment of shared joy during a painful time.

On the pitch, the story provides more specific things to examine: a possession plan suited to the team, a response to losing against England, and repeated recovery after falling behind in the final. Think about your own next difficult match. What action could help you remain useful to the team after a setback? A supporting run, a clear message or a secure pass is something you can choose, even while the result remains uncertain.

sections.heading: 1. An opportunity seen from a tram
sections.text:
Samira Hurem’s idea began with girls she could see playing football in parks as she travelled home from university by tram. They enjoyed the game, but lacked somewhere to train. In 2000, she helped turn that unmet need into SFK 2000 Sarajevo.

The early work was practical. She gathered players, taught football and found places to practise. Hurem later recalled sometimes being moved on by police. After the club became champions in its third season, she transferred from medical studies to sport, pursued coaching qualifications, and worked at a school and as a referee to help buy equipment. The club’s beginnings were about creating regular football before they were about collecting trophies. An opportunity had to be organised before it could be developed.

sections.heading: 2. Wanting stronger competition
sections.text:
A federation interview following the 2011/12 season reveals how Hurem understood progress. Sarajevo’s ambitions included domestic league and cup success and qualification for European competition. Yet she also wanted stronger opponents at home, improvements to the league structure and more opportunities for younger age groups.

Those aims belong together. A successful team needs a competition that makes its players think and adapt. In the interview, Hurem supported youth tournaments and festivals as places where players and clubs could meet and test their work. UEFA’s historical record later lists Sarajevo in the Champions League round of 32 in 2009/10, 2012/13, 2016/17 and 2018/19. Reaching that round was a European achievement, but it was not the same as winning the competition. Domestic success and continental progress need to be measured separately.

sections.heading: 3. Reading a championship carefully
sections.text:
On 6 June 2022, Bosnia and Herzegovina’s national federation reported Sarajevo’s twentieth national championship. Its account provides a revealing snapshot: after 20 matches, the team had 19 wins and one draw, with 58 points and a 14-point advantage over second-placed Emina. A final match still remained.

That last detail matters. The numbers describe the position when the article was published, not a complete final-season record. A careful reader should not silently turn 20 matches into the season’s total. Equally, the twentieth title was a national league championship, not a twentieth European trophy. Understanding the labels around an achievement lets us appreciate its scale without enlarging it into something else. The record was remarkable enough to deserve precision.

sections.heading: 1. A football instead of a doll
sections.text:
Rose Reilly grew up in Stewarton, Ayrshire, with an ambition that the adults around her did not always understand. As a child, she wanted a football for Christmas. When she received a doll instead, she found another child willing to swap. Her choice was already clear: she wanted to play.

At seven, she joined a boys’ team on the condition that she cut her hair and use the name Ross. A Celtic scout later noticed her ability, but discovering that she was a girl ended the possibility of signing her. These were barriers placed around a talented player before anyone could fairly test how far her football might take her. Being good enough did not guarantee access to the next opportunity.

sections.heading: 2. A corner kick for Scotland
sections.text:
Reilly went on to play for Stewarton Thistle Ladies. In November 1972, she represented Scotland against England at Ravenscraig Stadium in Greenock, in the first official women’s international between the countries. Scotland went two goals ahead, with Mary Carr and Reilly scoring. Reilly’s goal came directly from a corner.

England recovered to win 3–2. The defeat belongs in the story alongside the historic occasion and the unusual goal. Reilly had helped establish an international beginning, even though the result went against her team. Much later, in 2019, she was among the pioneers presented with a cap recognising that appearance. The gap between playing the match and receiving recognition shows how slowly football institutions sometimes acknowledged the women who had represented them.

sections.heading: 3. Learning a different game and language
sections.text:
To pursue professional football, Reilly travelled to France with fellow Scottish player Edna Neillis and earned an opportunity at Stade de Reims. A move to Milan followed. Leaving Scotland opened a route into football that she could not find at home, but moving abroad also brought unfamiliar daily challenges.

In an interview with Italian football historian Giovanni Di Salvo, she recalled living alone in a hotel and struggling to communicate: her teammates did not speak English, and she did not know Italian. She bought the pink sports newspaper La Gazzetta dello Sport and a dictionary, setting herself the task of learning three words each day. Teammates and everyday conversations helped too. Her adaptation involved listening and practising away from the pitch as well as on it.

sections.heading: 4. A ban, and a demanding double life
sections.text:
In 1975, the Scottish Women’s Football Association imposed a lifetime ban on Reilly. Accounts of the dispute describe her professional career abroad and disagreements with the association. The essential distinction is that this was exclusion by the Scottish women’s association, not a worldwide ban preventing her from playing club football elsewhere.

She continued building a career in Europe. The Scottish Sports Hall of Fame records that she won championships in both Italy and France during 1978–79, combining Lecce with Reims. Her own later interview also describes playing in Italy on Saturday before flying to France for another match. Sources differ over the precise season attached to this arrangement; the extraordinary cross-border commitment is much better established. It should not be mistaken for two international teams playing on the same weekend.

sections.heading: 5. Italy’s captain in 1984
sections.text:
The international opportunity that followed was particularly unusual. Reilly had already represented Scotland, yet she was selected to captain Italy at the 1984 Mundialito. Italy won the final against West Germany 3–1, and Reilly scored one of the goals. She was also voted the Italian team’s best player.

The tournament is often described as an unofficial women’s world cup. That description needs care: it was not the FIFA Women’s World Cup, which began in China in 1991. Recognising the difference does not diminish the football or the achievement. It places the victory in the international landscape that existed at the time. Reilly’s story crosses national boundaries, but the competition’s identity must stay clear when we describe what she won.

sections.heading: 6. More than one famous tournament
sections.text:
Her career cannot be reduced to that final. By retirement at forty, her record included eight Serie A championships and four Italian Cups. She twice finished as the Italian league’s leading scorer, with Golden Boot seasons in 1978 and 1981. Success came across different clubs and over many years.

For a developing player, those repeated achievements invite a different question from simply asking whether she was talented. What allowed that talent to remain useful across new teammates, languages and settings? The sources show a player who kept finding ways to participate. They do not prove that every move was easy or that determination alone removed discrimination. Her achievements required football opportunities abroad, alongside the ability and work she brought to them.

sections.heading: 7. Recognition, and the next player
sections.text:
Recognition in Scotland eventually became more visible. Reilly entered the Scottish sporting and football halls of fame in 2007. She became the first woman to receive the PFA Scotland Merit Award in 2011, and received an MBE for services to women’s football in the 2020 New Year Honours.

Her career asks us to think about opportunity as well as effort. A child should not have to hide being a girl to join a team, or leave her country simply to pursue a serious sporting ambition. sections.heading: 1. A ball in Bethlehem
sections.text:
Honey Thaljieh’s football began in the narrow streets of Bethlehem, in the occupied Palestinian territory. In her own account, she discovered the game at seven. Boys were playing nearby, and she wanted to join them. What she found was both enjoyment and a challenge to the expectations surrounding her.

There was no ready-made route through girls’ clubs, regular coaching and equipment. Football offered somewhere to express ability and confidence even when other parts of life felt restricted. Her childhood should not be imagined as a conventional academy journey with a few difficult matches added. The first problem was being allowed a place in the game at all. The next was turning occasional play into an opportunity that other girls could share.

sections.heading: 2. Different reactions within one family
sections.text:
Thaljieh has described resistance to girls playing football, including within her family. In a recorded interview, she remembered her mother’s encouragement and her father’s initial opposition. She questioned why her brothers could play outside while she was expected to remain at home.

The story is specific to the people and circumstances she describes. It should not become a claim that all Palestinian families reacted in the same way. Her father’s attitude later changed, and he became proud of her public achievements. That change matters because it shows how support can develop, rather than dividing everyone permanently into supporters and opponents. For a player, a helpful adult can make a practical difference by listening to what she wants and taking her ambition seriously.

sections.heading: 3. Founding a team was a different task
sections.text:
In 2003, Thaljieh helped establish the Palestinian women’s national team and became its first captain. This was collective work: calling her a co-founder recognises that she did not create women’s football alone. A captain needed teammates, and a team needed people willing to organise its activities.

In 2005, the players took part in the West Asian Football Federation Women’s Championship in Jordan. That sequence is important. Establishing the team and playing its early international competition were separate stages, two years apart. Neither should be confused with every later milestone in playing at home. Building something new often involves several beginnings: gathering players, preparing together, entering a competition and becoming visible to a wider public. One date rarely explains the whole process.

sections.heading: 4. Before the referee’s whistle
sections.text:
Getting players onto the same pitch was itself difficult. Thaljieh’s account describes checkpoints, travel restrictions and the separation of Palestinian communities interfering with training, selection and tournament journeys. A coach could not simply assume that every available player would reach a session on time.

These conditions affected more than convenience. When players cannot gather regularly, practising combinations and assessing the available talent becomes harder. That is a football consequence drawn from the restrictions she describes, not an excuse invented after a defeat. To understand a team fairly, we need to examine preparation as well as the scoreboard. Ask what happened before the whistle: who could attend, what facilities were available, and how consistently the group could work together. Those questions reveal opportunities that a result alone cannot measure.

sections.text:
Qatar’s 3-2-1 Olympic and Sports Museum has displayed Thaljieh’s red number 10 Palestine shirt, on loan from her, among objects representing major sporting careers. It provides a tangible record of a woman who helped make a national team possible. The shirt belongs to a history of participation and leadership, rather than a story built around winning a world championship.

Museum objects also ask us to be precise. A displayed shirt can document a player and her sporting identity; by itself, it does not establish every date, result or attendance connected with her career. Those details require other records. For this card, the shirt is a reminder that football heritage includes creating opportunities, not only the medals collected by already established teams.

sections.heading: 6. A career changes direction
sections.text:
A series of knee injuries ended Thaljieh’s competitive playing career. Her involvement in football continued through education and institutional work. These records trace a different kind of football contribution: studying how sport operates, communicating its work and speaking about access for women. Her later role did not make the injury unimportant. It showed that leaving competitive play did not have to end her relationship with the game.

Individual effort and a supportive environment work together. For a STAR player, the practical challenge is to identify one thing that helps you belong and one thing that could improve.
